Async TS and ES Modules

Build interactive CLI apps with modularity.

Welcome back. Today we move from static code to interactive, modular CLI applications using modern TypeScript.

Lecture Agenda

  • ES Module Syntax
  • Built-in vs Custom Modules
  • Asynchronous Flow
  • Promises and Await
  • Top-Level Await
  • CLI Application Building
  • TypeScript Configuration
We will cover how to organize code, handle user input, and configure our environment for modern standards.

The Power of Modularity

  • Scalability requires separate files
  • Avoid "God Files" with everything
  • Separate business logic from UI
  • Easier testing and maintenance
Modularity is the foundation of scalable software. We keep logic in one place and execution in another.

ES Module Syntax

  • Modern standard for Node.js
  • Replaces old CommonJS 'require'
  • Uses 'import' and 'export'
  • Cleaner and more efficient
We are moving away from require() to the standard ESM syntax used in modern web and server development.

Exporting Custom Modules

  • Use arrow functions for logic
  • Export specific named functions
  • Example: finance.ts logic
export const calculateTip = (total: number, percent: number) => total * (percent / 100);
export const calculateTotal = (total: number, tip: number) => total + tip;
In finance.ts, we define our math logic and export it so other files can use it.

Importing Custom Modules

  • Import specific functions by name
  • Must use .js extension
  • Even when writing in .ts
import { calculateTip, calculateTotal } from './finance.js';
A common gotcha: TypeScript requires the .js extension in the import path to match the final compiled output.

Node.js Built-in Modules

  • Use 'node:' prefix for safety
  • Modern best practice for Node
  • Access system-level functionality
import * as readline from 'node:readline/promises';
import { stdin as input, stdout as output } from 'node:process';
The node: prefix clarifies that we are using a built-in module rather than a package from npm.

Asynchronous Flow

  • User input is unpredictable
  • Programs must pause and wait
  • Prevents blocking the main thread
  • Essential for interactive CLI apps
Unlike math, user input doesn't happen instantly. We need patterns to handle this waiting period.

Promises Explained

  • Placeholder for future values
  • Represents an unfinished task
  • Can be Pending, Resolved, Rejected
  • Returned by modern Node APIs
Think of a Promise like a buzzer at a restaurant; it's a placeholder until your food (the data) is ready.

The Await Keyword

  • Halts execution until Promise resolves
  • Assigns result to a variable
  • Makes async code look linear
  • Simplifies complex callback logic
Await allows us to write code that reads top-to-bottom, even if it's waiting for a user to type.

Top-Level Await

  • Use await outside of functions
  • Requires ESNext configuration
  • No more wrapper functions needed
  • Standard for modern CLI scripts
Historically, we had to wrap everything in an async function. Now, we can use await at the root level.

TSConfig for Top-Level Await

  • Set target to ESNext
  • Set module to ESNext
  • Enable node module resolution
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ESNext",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "node",
    "types": ["node"]
  }
}
These settings are mandatory. Without ESNext, TypeScript will throw an error when using await at the top level.

Package.json Configuration

  • Must add "type": "module"
  • Enables ESM in Node.js
  • Prevents CommonJS errors
If you forget this step, Node will treat your files as old-style scripts and imports will fail.

Handling User Input

  • Use readline/promises for input
  • Always call rl.close()
  • Prevents CLI from hanging
const rl = readline.createInterface({ input, output });
const answer = await rl.question('Total? ');
rl.close();
Closing the interface is vital; otherwise, the terminal process will stay open forever.

Building the CLI App

  • Initialize the input stream
  • Prompt user for data
  • Process data with custom modules
  • Output the final result
We combine our finance logic with our readline interface to create a functional calculator.

Common Gotchas

  • Missing .js in import paths
  • Forgetting "type": "module"
  • Incorrect tsconfig target settings
  • Hanging processes (no rl.close)
Watch out for these four issues; they account for most beginner errors in this workflow.

Summary

  • Modularity ensures scalable code
  • Use ESM import/export syntax
  • Await handles unpredictable user input
  • Configure TSConfig for ESNext
  • Always close your input streams
Remember: separate your logic, use modern syntax, and always clean up your resources.
